prediction_ref.short_label: Agent-framework loaders ship signed-checkpoint and manifest mode by Q4 2026

validation_rows.evidence_summary: Palo Alto Unit 42's June 16 'Pickle in the Middle' disclosure is the strongest single-incident pull this prediction has had. The chain turns on the same mechanism the prediction targets: a model artifact serialized with pickle/joblib whose __reduce__ method executes arbitrary code the instant Google's Vertex serving container deserializes it, here escalated to cross-tenant RCE because the SDK verified only that a default staging bucket existed, not that the caller owned it. Google's shipped remediation path - UUID-randomized bucket names (v1.144.0) then full ownership verification (v1.148.0) - is exactly the signed/attested-provenance and caller-verification posture the prediction says loaders will default to, and a published cross-tenant break gives the broader framework cohort a citable reason to move artifact trust from opt-in to default.

prediction_ref.short_label: Open-source serving stacks ship signed-checkpoint loading as default by Q4 2026

validation_rows.evidence_summary: The Vertex AI pickle-deserialization RCE Unit 42 disclosed on June 16 is a direct demonstration of the failure mode this prediction's signed-load default is meant to close: an untrusted checkpoint runs code at load time inside a serving container. The deeper lesson the day's coverage draws is structural and not vendor-specific - managed-inference and model-serving platforms inherit Python's deserialization risk at the tenant boundary, and the clean mitigation is to stop trusting raw artifacts, favoring non-executable serialization (safetensors-class formats over pickle) plus signed/attested provenance. That is precisely the open-serving-stack default this prediction forecasts, and a concrete published break with a remediation Google already shipped raises the bar for peer serving stacks to follow.
